$comment: THE SHARED CLAUSE-TRUTH FIXTURE (plan 032 §5.5, §5.9; task 28).
One list of cases, read by BOTH implementations of `test_clause`: `automationClauseTruth.ts`
(jest) and `automation_engine/eval.rs` (cargo, via include_str!). The editor now draws a
per-clause verdict beside each row, and the engine decides whether the rule fires — two surfaces
describing one rule, which is the defect this milestone kept having to repair. Kleene's third
value, `f64` coercion and the comparison epsilon are exactly the things that drift silently, so
they are pinned case for case rather than trusted. `two-implementations-one-fix`.
`clause` is a COMPLETE `Clause` in the wire DTO's own spelling, so Rust reads it with
`serde_json::from_str` and no adapter, exactly as `automationValidationCases.json` does.
`caps` is the RENDERER's capture shape — `Record<string, string>`, what `sampleFromPattern`
returns — because that is what production feeds the TypeScript side. A key is present if and
only if the group PARTICIPATED, which is the same fact Rust's `Captures` carries as the
`Option` inside each slot: an absent key and a `None` slot read identically through
`Captures::group`/`name`, so the Rust side rebuilds a `Captures` from this map and nothing is
lost. `"1": ""` (present, empty) and a missing `"1"` (did not participate) are DIFFERENT
cases and both appear below — collapsing them is the M1 review's Important 1.
`expected` is `true` / `false` / `unknown` — `Truth`, three-valued. `unknown` is never `false`:
a clause that taught the read nothing must not decide the rule, and an OR chain may still carry
a row this one could not answer.
**The one divergence this fixture cannot close, said out loud.** A `matches` clause compiles its
own operand as a regex, with V8 in the renderer and the `regex` crate in the engine, and the two
accept different syntax — `(?<=a)b` compiles in V8 and not in `regex`. That gap is not new here:
`cond.badClausePattern` has it already (`compilePattern` on one side, `Regex::new` on the other)
and the validation fixture lives with it the same way. So no case below uses syntax only one
engine accepts; the `(?P<…>)` case is the opposite direction and IS pinned, because
`compilePattern`'s rescue exists to close that one.

cases.name: $0 contains the words it matched
$0 does not contain something else
an empty needle is contained by everything
cases.why: Rust's `str::contains("")` and JavaScript's `String.includes('')` are both true; a port that special-cased the empty operand would diverge here.

cases.name: notContains is the negation, not a second reading
notContains is false when it does contain it
is compares the whole token, not a prefix
is is false for a token that merely starts with the value
isNot is the negation of is
isNot is false when they are equal
a named group is read by its name
a text clause on a group that did not participate reads the empty string
cases.why: §5.5's asymmetry: a non-participating token is a KNOWN absence to a text test (§4.4), so isEmpty gets a real answer — `true`, not `unknown`.

cases.name: isNotEmpty on that same absent group is a known false
a name the pattern never declared reads the empty string too
cases.why: §5.5 draws no declared-vs-undeclared row: that is a validation problem (`cond.unknownToken`), not a case this function tells apart.

cases.name: a group that participated and captured nothing is empty, and that is not the same fact
isNotEmpty on a token that holds something
matches runs the clause's own pattern against the token
matches is unanchored on both sides
matches is false when the clause pattern does not find anything
a matches clause whose own pattern will not compile is unknown, never false
cases.why: A broken clause must not read as "no" — the same asymmetry a non-numeric token gets below.

cases.name: the `(?P<name>…)` spelling runs on both engines
cases.why: `regex` keeps it as its own historical spelling; V8 throws `Invalid group`. `compilePattern`'s rescue exists for exactly this, and this case is what holds the rescue in place.

cases.name: gt on a number the token holds
gt is false below the threshold
gte includes the boundary and gt does not
gt excludes that same boundary
lt below the threshold
lte includes the boundary
eq compares with an epsilon, never with ==
cases.why: 0.1 + 0.2 printed by a program and 0.3 typed by a user are two different f64s. An exact comparison reads `false` here, which is the silent failure the epsilon exists to prevent.

cases.name: neq is the epsilon's negation, so the same pair is not unequal
eq is false for numbers further apart than the epsilon
neq is true for those same two
a numeric clause with no threshold yet asks nothing and is told nothing
cases.why: `cond.clauseNeedsValue` blocks it, so only a hand-edited rule reaches here; reading it as `false` would let an unfinished comparison decide the rule.

cases.name: a numeric clause on a token that is not a number is unknown
a numeric clause on a group that did not participate is unknown
cases.why: This is the row the editor must NOT draw as a red cross: an OR chain may still carry it.

cases.name: surrounding whitespace is trimmed before coercion
an empty token is not the number zero
cases.why: `Number('')` is `0` in JavaScript and `"".parse::<f64>()` is an error in Rust. A port written with a bare `Number()` reads this `true` and fires a rule on a capture that holds nothing.

cases.name: hexadecimal is not a number here
cases.why: `Number('0x10')` is 16 in JavaScript; `"0x10".parse::<f64>()` is an error. The engine would never fire this and the editor must not say it would.

cases.name: a digit separator is not a number here
a value too large for f64 is not finite, so it is unknown
cases.why: Rust parses `1e400` to infinity and `is_finite` throws it out; JavaScript's `Number` gives `Infinity` and `Number.isFinite` throws it out. Both must refuse, or a runaway reading looks like a passing threshold.

cases.name: the word infinity is not a number here either
cases.why: `"Infinity".parse::<f64>()` succeeds in Rust and is then filtered by `is_finite`. The filter is what makes the two sides agree.

cases.name: a leading sign and an exponent are numbers on both sides
a trailing decimal point is a number on both sides
a leading decimal point is a number on both sides
a negative reading compares as a negative number
$0 can be compared numerically too
a named group can be compared numerically
a whole match that did not participate at all is unknown to a number test
cases.why: `sampleFromPattern` returning `{}` and returning `null` are different facts; this is the `{}` one, and it must not read as a comparison against zero.
